propositions.text: Transfer pricing issues arise when multinational entities transfer property or services without arm's length dealings, risking profit diversion.
propositions.quote: Transfer pricing issues arise when entities of multinational corporations resident in different jurisdictions transfer property or provide services to one another.

propositions.text: Since 1939, the Income Tax Act allows reassessment to include differences between non-arm's length prices and arm's length prices.
propositions.quote: Since 1939, the Income Tax Act has included provisions under which a Canadian taxpayer may be reassessed to include, in Canadian profits, the difference between the prices for property paid to a non-resident with which it does not deal at arm’s length and what those prices would have been had they been dealing at arm’s length.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains transfer pricing issues and the Income Tax Act's reassessment provisions since 1939.

propositions.text: The Minister reassessed Glaxo Canada for 1990-1993 under s. 69(2) for paying above arm's length prices for ranitidine.
propositions.quote: The Minister of National Revenue reassessed GlaxoSmithKline Inc. (“Glaxo Canada”) for the taxation years 1990, 1991, 1992, and 1993, pursuant to the then-applicable s. 69(2) of the Income Tax Act...

propositions.text: Tax Court upheld reassessment with minor revision; Federal Court of Appeal allowed appeal and remitted for reconsideration.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Canada appealed to the Tax Court of Canada, where Rip A.C.J. (as he then was) upheld, with one minor revision, the reassessment. On Glaxo Canada’s further appeal, the Federal Court of Appeal allowed the appeal and remitted the matter to the Tax Court for reconsideration.

propositions.text: The Minister appeals the Federal Court of Appeal decision to this Court.
propositions.quote: The Minister has appealed that decision to this Court.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister reassessed Glaxo Canada; Tax Court upheld; Federal Court of Appeal allowed appeal; Minister appeals to this Court.

propositions.text: The issue is the correct application of s. 69(2), especially what circumstances to consider in determining reasonable arm's length price.
propositions.quote: The issue on appeal is the correct application of s. 69(2) : in particular, what circumstances are to be taken into account in determining the reasonable arm’s length price against which to compare the non-arm’s length transfer price.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada cross-appeals the remittal, arguing no rehearing is needed as Minister's assumptions are demolished.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Canada cross-appeals the decision of the Federal Court of Appeal to remit the matter to the Tax Court for rehearing and reconsideration. If this Court denies the Minister’s appeal, Glaxo Canada argues that the matter should not be remitted because it has successfully demolished the Minister’s assumptions, thus fully discharging the taxpayer’s burden in appealing the reassessment.

propositions.text: The court would dismiss both the Minister's appeal and Glaxo Canada's cross-appeal.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I would dismiss both the appeal and the cross-appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue and notes Glaxo Canada's cross-appeal; the court would dismiss both appeals.

propositions.text: Between 1990-1993, Glaxo Canada bought ranitidine from related non-resident Adechsa at $1,512-$1,651/kg.
propositions.quote: Between 1990 and 1993, the respondent, Glaxo Canada, purchased ranitidine... from Adechsa S.A., a related non-resident company, for between $1,512 and $1,651 per kilogram.

propositions.text: Two Canadian generic companies bought ranitidine from other sources at $194-$304/kg during same period.
propositions.quote: During the same period, two Canadian generic pharmaceutical companies, Apotex Inc. and Novopharm Ltd., purchased ranitidine from other sources... for between $194 and $304 per kilogram.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Glaxo Canada bought ranitidine from related Adechsa at high prices; generics bought at much lower prices.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada was a wholly owned subsidiary of Glaxo Group Ltd., itself owned by Glaxo Holdings plc in the UK.
propositions.quote: At the relevant time Glaxo Canada was a wholly owned subsidiary of Glaxo Group Ltd., which itself was a wholly owned subsidiary of Glaxo Holdings plc, a United Kingdom corporation.

propositions.text: Glaxo Group owned companies that discovered, developed, manufactured, and marketed branded pharmaceuticals worldwide.
propositions.quote: In addition to its ownership of Glaxo Canada, Glaxo Group was the parent of other companies, which discovered, developed, manufactured and marketed branded pharmaceutical products.

propositions.text: Products were marketed worldwide through subsidiaries like Glaxo Canada or independent distributors.
propositions.quote: These products were then placed in a delivery mechanism such as a tablet, liquid or gel and marketed and sold throughout the world through subsidiaries such as Glaxo Canada or independent arm’s length distributors.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes Glaxo Canada's ownership and Glaxo Group's global pharmaceutical operations.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada acted as secondary manufacturer and marketer, acquiring ranitidine and marketing Zantac under licence.
propositions.quote: During the taxation years in issue, Glaxo Canada acted as a secondary manufacturer and marketer which meant that it acquired the active pharmaceutical ingredient, ranitidine, and put it into a delivery mechanism and packaged and marketed Zantac...

propositions.text: Glaxo Group owned Zantac trademark and patent, granting rights to Glaxo Canada under Licence Agreement.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Group owned the Zantac trademark and the patent for its active ingredient, ranitidine, and granted rights under the patent and trademark to Glaxo Canada under a Licence Agreement.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada purchased ranitidine from Adechsa under a Supply Agreement.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Canada purchased ranitidine from Adechsa, a Glaxo Group clearing company located in Switzerland, under a Supply Agreement.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Glaxo Canada's role, licence rights, and ranitidine purchase from Adechsa under agreements.

propositions.text: The Licence Agreement granted Glaxo Canada multiple rights including patents, trademarks, technical assistance, marketing support, indemnification, and sublicensing.
propositions.quote: At the heart of this appeal are these two agreements. The Licence Agreement conferred the following rights and benefits on Glaxo Canada: 1. the right under the patents to manufacture, use and sell Glaxo Group products...

paragraphs.summary: The court lists the extensive rights and benefits granted to Glaxo Canada under the Licence Agreement.

propositions.text: Under the Supply Agreement, transfer prices for ranitidine were set using the resale-price method with a 60% gross margin for distributors.
propositions.quote: Under the Supply Agreement, Glaxo Group set the transfer prices of the active ingredient, ranitidine, using the resale-price method as described by Rip A.C.J....

propositions.text: This method resulted in prices over $1,500/kg for ranitidine paid by Glaxo Canada to Adechsa.
propositions.quote: This method resulted in prices of over $1,500 per kilogram for ranitidine paid by Glaxo Canada to Adechsa.

propositions.text: Combined Licence and Supply agreements enabled Glaxo Canada to purchase ranitidine, package, and market it under Zantac trademark.
propositions.quote: The combined effect of the Licence and Supply agreements enabled Glaxo Canada, among other things, to purchase the active ingredient ranitidine, put it in a delivery mechanism, and market it under the trademark Zantac.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the resale-price method for transfer pricing and combined effect of Licence and Supply agreements.

propositions.text: Apotex and Novopharm sold generic anti-ulcer drugs, buying ranitidine at $194-$304/kg from arm's length suppliers.
propositions.quote: During the taxation years in issue, two Canadian generic pharmaceutical companies, Apotex and Novopharm, sold generic anti-ulcer pharmaceutical products in Canada. These companies purchased ranitidine at lower prices than Glaxo Canada, between $194 and $304 per kilogram, from arm’s length suppliers.

propositions.text: No evidence showed generic companies' supply contracts conferred benefits beyond ranitidine supply.
propositions.quote: There was no evidence that the supply contracts of Apotex or Novopharm conferred anything beyond the supply of ranitidine.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes generic companies bought ranitidine cheaper from arm's length suppliers without additional benefits.

propositions.text: Generic companies marketed patented drugs under compulsory licensing scheme existing until Feb 1993, paying royalties to patent owners.
propositions.quote: These generic companies were able to market generic versions of drugs whose patent was still in effect by reason of the compulsory licensing scheme that existed for pharmaceutical products in Canada up to February 1993...

propositions.text: Licences granted before Dec 20, 1991, continued despite repeal of compulsory licensing in 1993.
propositions.quote: The licences granted to Apotex and Novopharm predated December 20, 1991, and therefore continued to subsist, notwithstanding repeal of the compulsory licensing scheme in February 1993...

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the compulsory licensing scheme allowing generics to market patented drugs with royalties until 1993.

propositions.text: Minister reassessed Glaxo Canada for 1990-1993, increasing income by $51 million under s. 69(2) for overpayment for ranitidine.
propositions.quote: The Minister reassessed Glaxo Canada for its 1990, 1991, 1992, and 1993 taxation years, increasing its income by some $51 million under s. 69(2) of the Act on the basis that it had paid Adechsa more than a reasonable amount for the purchase of ranitidine.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Minister reassessed Glaxo Canada by $51 million for overpaying for ranitidine.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. affirmed the Minister’s reassessment and found Singleton required Licence and Supply agreements to be considered independently.
propositions.quote: Rip A.C.J. affirmed the Minister’s reassessment. He found that Singleton v. Canada... required the Licence and Supply agreements to be considered independently.

propositions.text: He did not consider Licence Agreement rights relevant to determining arm’s length price for ranitidine supply.
propositions.quote: As a result, he did not consider whether the rights and benefits under the Licence Agreement were a relevant circumstance in determining the appropriate arm’s length price for the supply of ranitidine.

paragraphs.summary: The Tax Court judge affirmed reassessment, finding Licence and Supply agreements must be considered independently and Licence Agreement irrelevant.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. used the comparable uncontrolled price (CUP) method per OECD Guidelines to test reasonableness of ranitidine prices.
propositions.quote: Rip A.C.J. employed the comparable uncontrolled price (“CUP”) method... to test the reasonableness of Glaxo Canada’s ranitidine transactions.

propositions.text: He found highest price paid by generic companies was appropriate comparator and Glaxo Canada paid more than reasonable amount.
propositions.quote: He found that the appropriate comparator transaction was the highest price paid by the generic pharmaceutical companies for ranitidine from arm’s length suppliers. Under this approach, he found the prices Glaxo Canada paid to Adechsa for ranitidine were greater than the reasonable amount had they been dealing at arm’s length.

propositions.text: He upheld reassessment except for a $25/kg increment for granulation.
propositions.quote: Aside from allowing a $25 per kilogram increment for granulation, he upheld the reassessment of the Minister.

paragraphs.summary: The Tax Court used CUP method, found Glaxo Canada paid more than reasonable, and upheld reassessment with minor allowance.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal found Tax Court erred by not considering Licence Agreement in price reasonableness under s. 69(2).
propositions.quote: Nadon J.A., writing for a unanimous panel, found that the Tax Court had erred in not considering the Licence Agreement when determining whether the prices paid by Glaxo Canada for ranitidine were reasonable under s. 69(2) .

propositions.text: Singleton was not relevant; test includes all circumstances an arm’s length purchaser would consider.
propositions.quote: He said that Singleton was not relevant and that the test of “reasonable in the circumstances” included all circumstances that an arm’s length purchaser would have to consider.

propositions.text: Adopted “reasonable business person” test from Gabco Ltd. requiring inquiry into relevant circumstances for price decision.
propositions.quote: Based on Gabco Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue... Nadon J.A. adopted the “reasonable business person” test, which required an inquiry into the circumstances that an arm’s length purchaser would consider relevant when deciding what price to pay.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. erred by assessing fair market value based on generic companies’ prices.
propositions.quote: He found that Rip A.C.J. had erred when he assessed the “fair market value” of ranitidine based on the amounts paid by the generic pharmaceutical companies to arm’s length suppliers.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court of Appeal found Tax Court erred by ignoring Licence Agreement and adopting a flawed comparator, applying the reasonable business person test.

propositions.text: Licence Agreement was central to Glaxo Canada’s business reality and a relevant circumstance even if Adechsa was arm’s length.
propositions.quote: Having determined that Singleton did not preclude looking at both the Supply and Licence agreements and applying the “reasonable business person” test, Justice Nadon found that the Licence Agreement was central to Glaxo Canada’s business reality, and that it would be so even if the relationship with Adechsa was at arm’s length.

propositions.text: Licence Agreement created fundamentally different circumstances, so generic companies’ prices were inappropriate comparators.
propositions.quote: Therefore, it was a “circumstance” that had to be taken into account when determining whether the prices paid by Glaxo Canada for ranitidine were reasonable. In his view, the Tax Court erred in using the purchase prices of ranitidine of the generic pharmaceutical companies to determine whether the Glaxo Canada prices were reasonable, as the Licence Agreement created fundamentally different circumstances for Glaxo Canada’s transactions.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court of Appeal found the Licence Agreement central and that generic prices were inappropriate comparators due to different circumstances.

propositions.text: Taxpayer had not fully discharged burden; reasonable amount for ranitidine transactions remained to be determined.
propositions.quote: However, Nadon J.A. found that the burden on the taxpayer had not been fully discharged as the “reasonable amount” remained to be determined for Glaxo Canada’s ranitidine transactions.

propositions.text: Matter remitted to Tax Court for redetermination.
propositions.quote: He remitted the matter to the Tax Court for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court of Appeal found the taxpayer had not discharged burden and remitted the matter for redetermination.

propositions.text: Transfer pricing provisions first enacted in 1939 and re-enacted with minor changes through 1985.
propositions.quote: The first transfer pricing provision in the Canadian Income Tax Act was enacted as s. 23B of the Income War Tax Act...

paragraphs.summary: The court outlines the history of transfer pricing provisions in the Income Tax Act since 1939.

propositions.text: 1985 version of s. 69(2) defines reasonable amount as what would be reasonable if dealing at arm’s length.
propositions.quote: The 1985 version of s. 69(2) applicable to the years 1990-1993 reads: (2) Where a taxpayer has paid or agreed to pay to a non-resident person with whom the taxpayer was not dealing at arm’s length...

paragraphs.summary: The court quotes s. 69(2) defining reasonable amount for non-arm’s length payments.

propositions.text: The section requires finding an arm’s length proxy replicating Glaxo Canada’s circumstances for ranitidine acquisition.
propositions.quote: On the facts of this case, the section asks whether the prices Glaxo Canada paid Adechsa for ranitidine were greater than what would have been reasonable if Adechsa and Glaxo Canada had been dealing at arm’s length.

propositions.text: Challenge is to find arm’s length proxy closely replicating Glaxo Canada’s acquisition circumstances.
propositions.quote: The challenge is to find an arm’s length proxy that replicates the circumstances of Glaxo Canada as closely as possible in respect of its acquisition of ranitidine.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue is finding an arm’s length proxy replicating Glaxo Canada’s circumstances for ranitidine purchase.

propositions.text: 1979 and 1995 OECD Guidelines provide commentary and methodology on transfer pricing but are not controlling law.
propositions.quote: In the courts below and in this Court, there has been reference to the 1979 Guidelines and the 1995 Guidelines (the “Guidelines”). The Guidelines contain commentary and methodology pertaining to the issue of transfer pricing.

propositions.text: The test of transactions or prices must be determined according to s. 69(2), not OECD Guidelines.
propositions.quote: However, the Guidelines are not controlling as if they were a Canadian statute and the test of any set of transactions or prices ultimately must be determined according to s. 69(2) rather than any particular methodology or commentary set out in the Guidelines.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes OECD Guidelines provide guidance but s. 69(2) governs transfer pricing tests.

propositions.text: Section 69(2) does not specify how to determine the reasonable amount payable at arm's length, but Guidelines suggest methods for transfer pricing consistency.
propositions.quote: Section 69(2) does not, itself, offer guidance as to how to determine the “reasonable amount” that would have been payable had the parties been dealing at arm’s length. However, the Guidelines suggest a number of methods for determining whether transfer prices are consistent with prices determined between parties dealing at arm’s length.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s.69(2) lacks guidance on reasonable amount determination, but Guidelines suggest methods for transfer pricing consistency.

propositions.text: In Tax Court, parties relied on four Guidelines methods to assess Glaxo Canada's prices to Adechsa; Minister used CUP and cost plus methods.
propositions.quote: In the Tax Court, the parties relied on four methods from the Guidelines to assess the reasonableness of the prices Glaxo Canada paid Adechsa. The Minister relied on the CUP method and the cost plus method (see 1979 Guidelines, at paras. 48 and 63).

propositions.text: CUP method compares prices in comparable arm's length transactions with taxpayer's transfer prices; it's the most direct way to determine arm's length price.
propositions.quote: The CUP method compares the prices in comparable transactions between parties dealing at arm’s length with the transfer prices paid by the taxpayer being reassessed. The Guidelines say this is the most direct way of determining the arm’s length price.

propositions.text: Minister compared Glaxo Canada's transfer prices with prices paid by Apotex and Novopharm using CUP method.
propositions.quote: This is the method under which the Minister compared the Glaxo Canada transfer prices with the prices paid by Apotex and Novopharm.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains parties used four methods; Minister used CUP and cost plus, CUP compares arm's length prices and was used to compare Glaxo Canada with Apotex and Novopharm.

propositions.text: 1995 Guidelines require arm's length transactions to be comparable, with no material price-affecting differences or adjustments to eliminate such effects.
propositions.quote: However, the 1995 Guidelines also say that the arm’s length transactions must be carefully considered for comparability with the transfer price transactions. Transactions are only comparable if: 1. None of the differences (if any) between the transactions being compared or between the enterprises undertaking those transactions could materially affect the price in the open market; or 2. Reasonably accurate adjustments can be made to eliminate the material effects of such differences. (See 1995 Guidelines, at para. 1.15.)

paragraphs.summary: The court states 1995 Guidelines require arm's length transactions to be comparable with no material price differences or adjustments to eliminate them.

propositions.text: Cost plus method is based on foreign suppliers' costs plus mark-up but has problems assessing costs and mark-up; useful to verify prices after other methods.
propositions.quote: The cost plus method is based upon the foreign suppliers’ costs, plus an appropriate mark-up. However, the 1979 Guidelines say that the method “raise[d] problems both as regards assessing costs . . . and the appropriate mark-up for profit” (para. 63). They suggest its usefulness may be as a means of verifying prices after other methods have been applied.

propositions.text: Minister used cost plus method to verify arm's length prices determined under CUP method.
propositions.quote: The Minister used the cost plus method to verify the arm’s length prices he determined under the CUP method.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains cost plus method's basis and problems; Minister used it to verify CUP method prices.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada relied on resale price, transactional net margin, and CUP methods using European comparators.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Canada relied on the resale price, the transactional net margin and the CUP methods, using a set of European comparators.

propositions.text: Resale-price method starts with reseller's market price, reduces by reseller's cost and profit margin to find transfer price, then compares gross profit margin to independent resellers.
propositions.quote: As described above, the resale-price method starts with the price charged by the reseller (Glaxo Canada) in the market for the product (Zantac). The price is then reduced by the proportion representing the reseller’s cost and appropriate profit, i.e. the reseller’s gross profit margin. The balance is the transfer price for the product purchased from the related non-resident supplier (Adechsa). This gross profit margin is then compared to the gross profit margin earned by independent arm’s length resellers.

propositions.text: 1979 Guidelines say resale-price method is most useful when applied to marketing operations.
propositions.quote: The 1979 Guidelines observe that this method is the most useful when applied to marketing operations.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada compared its gross profit margin with independent European distributors of Zantac.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Canada compared its gross profit margin with those of independent European distributors of Zantac.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes Glaxo Canada's use of resale price, transactional net margin, and CUP methods with European comparators and explains resale-price method.

propositions.text: Transactional net margin method compares net profit relative to costs, sales or assets in controlled transactions to comparable uncontrolled transactions or independent enterprises with adjustments.
propositions.quote: The transactional net margin method looks at the net profit relative to a base such as costs, sales or assets in a controlled transaction as compared to the net profit ratio earned by the same taxpayer in comparable uncontrolled transactions. If this is not possible, consideration may be given to the net profit relative to costs, sales or assets of an independent enterprise, provided the circumstances are comparable and adjustments may be made to obtain reliable results.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains transactional net margin method compares net profit ratios in controlled and comparable uncontrolled transactions or independent enterprises.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada's CUP approach used prices paid by European independent distributors of Zantac, which approximated prices paid to Adechsa.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Canada’s CUP approach utilized the prices paid by European independent distributors of Zantac which Glaxo Canada submitted approximated the prices paid by Glaxo Canada to Adechsa.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Glaxo Canada's CUP approach used European independent distributors' prices approximating those paid to Adechsa.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. rejected Glaxo Canada's evidence and compared prices paid by Glaxo Canada and Canadian generic companies, finding Glaxo paid over $1,500/kg vs. $300/kg for generics.
propositions.quote: Rip A.C.J. rejected Glaxo Canada’s evidence and submissions. Utilizing the CUP method, Rip A.C.J. compared the prices paid by Glaxo Canada with those paid by the Canadian generic companies for ranitidine and found that the highest generic prices paid were in the range of $300 per kilogram, while Glaxo Canada was paying over $1,500 per kilogram.

paragraphs.summary: Rip A.C.J. rejected Glaxo Canada's evidence and found Glaxo paid much higher prices than Canadian generics using CUP method.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada argued comparison with generic companies was inappropriate because Licence Agreement conferred rights and benefits related to ranitidine purchase purpose.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Canada had argued that the comparison with generic companies was inappropriate. It said that the Licence Agreement must be taken into account, as it conferred certain rights and benefits related to the purpose for which its ranitidine was purchased.

paragraphs.summary: Glaxo Canada argued comparison with generics was inappropriate due to Licence Agreement rights and benefits.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. found Singleton precluded considering Licence Agreement; prices under Supply Agreement were only for ranitidine without compensation for other rights.
propositions.quote: However, Rip A.C.J. found that Singleton precluded him from considering the Licence Agreement. Absent the Licence Agreement, the prices paid under the Supply Agreement had to be considered as being only for ranitidine. There could thus be no compensation for other rights or benefits under the Supply Agreement.

propositions.text: Because prices paid by Glaxo Canada and generics were solely for ranitidine, no differences justified higher transfer prices except $25/kg granulation charge allowed to Glaxo Canada.
propositions.quote: Because the prices paid by Glaxo Canada and the generic companies were both solely for ranitidine, there were no differences between the transactions that might justify higher transfer prices than the prices paid by Apotex and Novopharm (aside from a $25 per kilogram charge for granulation that Glaxo Canada was allowed).

paragraphs.summary: Rip A.C.J. found Singleton barred considering Licence Agreement; prices were only for ranitidine with no differences justifying higher prices except $25/kg granulation charge.

propositions.text: The question before Rip A.C.J. was determining reasonable price under s. 69(2), focusing on whether Licence Agreement was a circumstance to consider.
propositions.quote: The question before Rip A.C.J. was the determination of the reasonable price under s. 69(2) . Critical to that determination was whether the Licence Agreement was a circumstance to be taken into account.

paragraphs.summary: Rip A.C.J. had to determine reasonable price under s.69(2), focusing on Licence Agreement's relevance.

propositions.text: Minister argues Singleton, Shell, and Guidelines require transactional approach treating each transfer separately, making Licence Agreement irrelevant.
propositions.quote: The Minister argues that this Court’s decisions in Singleton and Shell Canada Ltd. v. Canada, [1999] 3 S.C.R. 622, along with the Guidelines, require a transactional, sometimes called a transaction-by-transaction, approach when determining the reasonable transfer price under s. 69(2) . In the Tax Court, the Minister explained that the transaction-by-transaction approach is one in which the transaction in issue must be considered independently from surrounding circumstances, other transactions, or other realities. In this Court, the Minister submitted that “each transfer is to be treated as a separate transaction” (A.F., at para. 46). Accordingly, the Licence Agreement would be irrelevant. (1) Singleton

paragraphs.summary: Minister argues Singleton, Shell, and Guidelines require transaction-by-transaction approach, making Licence Agreement irrelevant.

propositions.text: Minister submits Singleton and Shell under s.20(1)(c)(i) require transaction-by-transaction approach under s.69(2).
propositions.quote: The Minister submits that Singleton and Shell, decided under s. 20(1) (c)(i) of the Act , are authority for the proposition that a transaction-by-transaction approach must be followed under s. 69(2) . Singleton involved the deductibility from income of interest paid and payable on borrowed money under s. 20(1) (c)(i), of the Income Tax Act .

propositions.text: Singleton involved borrowed funds used for earning income; borrowing to replenish capital account was separate from withdrawing funds to buy a house.
propositions.quote: In Singleton, the taxpayer used funds from his capital account at his law firm to assist in financing the purchase of a home. He then used borrowed funds to replace the funds he was withdrawing from his capital account. The sole issue was whether borrowed money was “used for the purpose of earning income”. This Court found that the borrowed funds were used to invest in the law firm for the purpose of earning income and, therefore, the interest payable thereon was deductible for income tax purposes. The fact that the borrowing occurred because the taxpayer wanted to use his equity in the firm to buy a house was irrelevant for determining the use of the borrowed funds. For purposes of s. 20(1) (c)(i), it would be wrong to collapse the transaction withdrawing funds from the firm to purchase the house and the borrowing transaction to replenish the capital account at the firm. It was the requirement to treat the two transactions separately that caused Rip A.C.J., at para. 78, to say that s. 69(2) required the Supply and Licence agreements to be treated separately.

paragraphs.summary: Minister submits Singleton and Shell under s.20(1)(c)(i) require transaction-by-transaction approach under s.69(2); Singleton involved separate borrowing and fund use transactions.

propositions.text: Tax Court judge and Minister ignore difference between s.20(1)(c)(i) and s.69(2).
propositions.quote: With respect, the approach of the Tax Court judge and the argument of the Minister ignore the difference between s. 20(1) (c)(i) and s. 69(2) .

propositions.text: Section 20(1)(c)(i) only requires factual determination of use of borrowed funds for earning income.
propositions.quote: Nothing in s. 20(1) (c)(i) entitles a court to search for anything other than the use to which the borrowed funds are put. The factual determination is simply whether the use of borrowed funds was for the purpose of earning income.

paragraphs.summary: The court says Tax Court judge and Minister ignore difference between s.20(1)(c)(i) and s.69(2); s.20(1)(c)(i) only requires factual use determination.

propositions.text: Section 20(1)(c)(i) does not require reasonableness or transaction comparison; s.69(2) requires determining if transfer price was reasonable considering arm's length parties and other transactions.
propositions.quote: Section 20(1) (c)(i) does not ask whether it is unreasonable to claim the interest deduction; nor does it require a comparison of transactions to determine if the deduction is reasonable. By contrast, s. 69(2) requires the court to determine whether the transfer price was greater than the amount that would have been reasonable in the circumstances, had the parties been dealing at arm’s length. If transactions other than the purchasing transaction are relevant in determining this question, they must not be ignored.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s.20(1)(c)(i) does not require reasonableness or transaction comparison, but s.69(2) does.

propositions.text: Shell involved borrowed funds converted to US currency and foreign currency transactions reducing effective interest rate while claiming deduction on initial rate.
propositions.quote: In Shell, the taxpayer had entered into an agreement to borrow $150 million in New Zealand currency at an interest rate of 15.4 percent. The taxpayer converted these funds into U.S. currency, which was then used for business purposes. Through a series of foreign currency transactions relating to the devaluation of the New Zealand currency over the course of the loan, Shell was able to reduce its effective rate of interest to 9.1 percent, while still claiming an income tax deduction based on the 15.4 percent interest rate on the initial transaction.

paragraphs.summary: Minister describes Shell case involving currency conversion and interest rate reduction while claiming deduction on initial rate.

propositions.text: Shell Court found conversion irrelevant to use of borrowed funds for earning income; Minister cannot re-characterize bona fide legal relationships.
propositions.quote: The Court found that it was irrelevant that the funds had been converted into U.S. currency as part of a sophisticated tax scheme. The Minister was not entitled to re-characterize the taxpayer’s bona fide legal relationships.

paragraphs.summary: Shell Court found currency conversion irrelevant to borrowed funds' use; Minister cannot re-characterize bona fide legal relationships.

propositions.text: Section 69(2) requires redetermining price as if between arm's length parties; other transactions may be relevant and must not be ignored, unlike Shell.
propositions.quote: The requirement of s. 69(2) is that the price established in a non-arm’s length transfer pricing transaction is to be redetermined as if it were between parties dealing at arm’s length. If the circumstances require, transactions other than the purchasing transactions must be taken into account to determine whether the actual price was or was not greater than the amount that would have been reasonable had the parties been dealing at arm’s length. Shell is therefore also inapplicable to a determination under s. 69(2) .

paragraphs.summary: The court states s.69(2) requires redetermining price as if arm's length parties, considering other transactions if relevant; Shell is inapplicable.

propositions.text: Minister relied on para.1.42 of 1995 Guidelines to justify transaction-by-transaction approach excluding Licence Agreement.
propositions.quote: The Minister also relied on para. 1.42 of the 1995 Guidelines to justify the transaction-by-transaction requirement. Paragraph 1.42 provides: Ideally, in order to arrive at the most precise approximation of fair market value, the arm’s length principle should be applied on a transaction-by-transaction basis. The Minister submits that para. 1.42 requires the court to focus only on the particular transaction at issue and, thus, does not permit the Licence Agreement to inform the determination of the reasonableness of the prices paid for ranitidine under the Supply Agreement.

paragraphs.summary: Minister relies on 1995 Guidelines para.1.42 to justify transaction-by-transaction approach excluding Licence Agreement.

propositions.text: Para.1.42 of 1995 Guidelines recognizes transaction-by-transaction approach is ideal but not appropriate in all cases when transactions are closely linked or continuous.
propositions.quote: However, para. 1.42 is not as restrictive as the Minister submits. It also provides: . . . there are often situations where separate transactions are so closely linked or continuous that they cannot be evaluated adequately on a separate basis. Thus, while a transaction-by-transaction approach may be ideal, the 1995 Guidelines themselves recognize that it is not appropriate in all cases.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains para.1.42 of 1995 Guidelines allows exceptions to transaction-by-transaction approach when transactions are closely linked.

propositions.text: 1995 Guidelines say arm’s length principle compares controlled transactions to independent enterprises’ transactions.
propositions.quote: Application of the arm’s length principle is generally based on a comparison of the conditions in a controlled transaction with the conditions in transactions between independent enterprises.

propositions.text: Economically relevant characteristics must be sufficiently comparable or adjustments made.
propositions.quote: To be comparable means that none of the differences (if any) between the situations being compared could materially affect the condition being examined in the methodology (e.g. price or margin), or that reasonably accurate adjustments can be made to eliminate the effect of any such differences.

paragraphs.summary: The 1995 Guidelines require arm’s length comparisons to consider sufficiently comparable economically relevant characteristics or make adjustments, prior court or authority says.

propositions.text: Proper arm’s length application requires regard to economically relevant characteristics to ensure comparability.
propositions.quote: a proper application of the arm’s length principle requires that regard be had for the “economically relevant characteristics” of the arm’s length and non-arm’s length circumstances to ensure they are “sufficiently comparable”.

propositions.text: Transaction-by-transaction approach may be appropriate if no related transactions or irrelevant related transactions.
propositions.quote: Where there are no related transactions or where related transactions are not relevant to the determination of the reasonableness of the price in issue, a transaction-by-transaction approach may be appropriate.

propositions.text: Economically relevant characteristics may require considering other transactions impacting the transfer price.
propositions.quote: “economically relevant characteristics of the situations being compared” may make it necessary to consider other transactions that impact the transfer price under consideration.

propositions.text: Whether to consider other transactions depends on relevant circumstances.
propositions.quote: In each case, it is necessary to address this question by considering the relevant circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains arm’s length principle requires considering economically relevant characteristics and possibly other transactions depending on circumstances.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. erred in finding he was precluded from considering the Licence Agreement.
propositions.quote: Rip A.C.J. was in error when he found that he was precluded from considering the Licence Agreement.

propositions.text: Whether Rip A.C.J. should have considered the Licence Agreement remains open.
propositions.quote: the question still remains as to whether he should have considered it.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Rip A.C.J. erred in excluding the Licence Agreement but whether it should have been considered remains.

propositions.text: Section 69(2) requires inquiry into reasonable price had parties dealt at arm’s length, considering all relevant circumstances.
propositions.quote: s. 69(2) requires an inquiry into the price that would be reasonable in the circumstances had the non-resident supplier and the Canadian taxpayer been dealing at arm’s length

propositions.text: Circumstances include linked agreements conferring rights and benefits beyond property purchase.
propositions.quote: Such circumstances will include agreements that may confer rights and benefits in addition to the purchase of property where those agreements are linked to the purchasing agreement.

propositions.text: Objective is to determine what arm’s length purchaser would pay for property and linked rights and benefits together.
propositions.quote: The objective is to determine what an arm’s length purchaser would pay for the property and the rights and benefits together where the rights and benefits are linked to the price paid for the property.

paragraphs.summary: Section 69(2) requires considering all circumstances, including linked agreements, to find what an arm’s length purchaser would pay.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada’s business was secondary manufacturing and marketing of brand-name pharmaceuticals including Zantac.
propositions.quote: The business of Glaxo Canada was the secondary manufacturing and marketing of brand-name pharmaceuticals, including Zantac.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada engaged in R&D but not related to Zantac.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Canada also engaged in research and development although there is no indication that its research and development work pertained to Zantac.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada’s purchase of ranitidine must be understood in light of its business reality.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Canada’s purchase of ranitidine must be understood, having regard to this business reality.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Glaxo Canada’s business was secondary manufacturing and marketing, with unrelated R&D, relevant to understanding its ranitidine purchase.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. found Licence Agreement required appellant to purchase ranitidine from Glaxo approved sources.
propositions.quote: Rip A.C.J. found, at para. 86, that “it was by virtue of the Licence Agreement that the appellant was required to purchase its ranitidine from Glaxo approved sources”.

propositions.text: Parties do not dispute Rip A.C.J.’s finding on Licence Agreement purchase requirement.
propositions.quote: The parties have not disputed this finding.

paragraphs.summary: Rip A.C.J. found appellant had to buy ranitidine from Glaxo approved sources under Licence Agreement; parties do not dispute this.

propositions.text: Only two approved sources existed, one being Adechsa.
propositions.quote: There were only two approved sources, one of which was Adechsa.

propositions.text: To benefit from Licence Agreement, Glaxo Canada had to buy active ingredient from these sources.
propositions.quote: in order to avail itself of the benefits of the Licence Agreement, Glaxo Canada was required to purchase the active ingredient from one of these sources.

propositions.text: Requirement arose from Glaxo Group’s control of trademark and patent, not from non-arm’s length relationship.
propositions.quote: This requirement was not the product of the non-arm’s length relationship between Glaxo Canada and Glaxo Group or Adechsa. Rather, it arose because Glaxo Group controlled the trademark and patent of the brand-name pharmaceutical product Glaxo Canada wished to market.

propositions.text: An arm’s length distributor might face the same requirement to purchase from approved sources.
propositions.quote: An arm’s length distributor wishing to market Zantac might well be faced with the same requirement.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Glaxo Canada had to buy from two approved sources due to Glaxo Group’s trademark control, a requirement an arm’s length distributor might face.

propositions.text: Link between Licence and Supply agreements means marketing Zantac involves contractual terms affecting ranitidine price not faced by generic marketers.
propositions.quote: The effect of the link between the Licence and Supply agreements was that an entity that wished to market Zantac was subject to contractual terms affecting the price of ranitidine that generic marketers of ranitidine products were not.

paragraphs.summary: The Licence and Supply agreements link imposes contractual terms on Zantac marketers affecting ranitidine price, unlike generic marketers.

propositions.text: Rights and benefits of Licence Agreement contingent on Glaxo Canada entering Supply Agreement with Glaxo Group designated suppliers.
propositions.quote: the rights and benefits of the Licence Agreement were contingent on Glaxo Canada entering into a Supply Agreement with suppliers to be designated by Glaxo Group.

propositions.text: Price paid allocated compensation to Glaxo Canada for secondary manufacturing and marketing function.
propositions.quote: The result of the price paid was to allocate to Glaxo Canada what Glaxo Group considered to be appropriate compensation for its secondary manufacturing and marketing function in respect of ranitidine and Zantac.

paragraphs.summary: Licence Agreement rights depend on Supply Agreement with Glaxo Group suppliers; price allocates compensation for Glaxo Canada’s manufacturing and marketing.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. was concerned multinational could avoid arm’s length pricing by requiring Canadian subsidiary to buy from specified supplier.
propositions.quote: Rip A.C.J. appears to have been concerned that a multinational organization, by requiring a Canadian subsidiary to acquire a product from a specified supplier, would escape the requirement to have its prices measured against arm’s length prices (para. 89).

propositions.text: Whatever price Glaxo Group sets is subject to s. 69(2) and arm’s length pricing requirement.
propositions.quote: whatever price was determined by Glaxo Group would be subject to s. 69(2) and the requirement that the transfer pricing transactions be measured against transactions between parties dealing with each other at arm’s length.

paragraphs.summary: Rip A.C.J. worried about avoiding arm’s length pricing, but court says all prices remain subject to s. 69(2) and arm’s length rules.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada paid for some Licence Agreement rights as part of ranitidine purchase price from Adechsa.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Canada was paying for at least some of the rights and benefits under the Licence Agreement as part of the purchase prices for ranitidine from Adechsa.

propositions.text: Licence Agreement cannot be ignored in determining reasonable amount paid under s. 69(2).
propositions.quote: the Licence Agreement could not be ignored in determining the reasonable amount paid to Adechsa under s. 69(2), which applies not only to payment for goods but also to payment for services.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Licence Agreement rights included in ranitidine price and must be considered under s. 69(2).

propositions.text: Considering Licence and Supply agreements together gives realistic picture of Glaxo Canada’s profits.
propositions.quote: Considering the Licence and Supply agreements together offers a realistic picture of the profits of Glaxo Canada.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada’s function was secondary manufacturing and marketing, not product origination or associated risks.
propositions.quote: It cannot be irrelevant that Glaxo Canada’s function was primarily as a secondary manufacturer and marketer. It did not originate new products and the intellectual property rights associated with them. Nor did it undertake the investment and risk involved with originating new products.

propositions.text: Glaxo Group undertook risks and investment costs under Licence Agreement.
propositions.quote: Nor did it have the other risks and investment costs which Glaxo Group undertook under the Licence Agreement.

propositions.text: Prices paid by Glaxo Canada to Adechsa pay for bundle of rights and benefits under Licence Agreement and product under Supply Agreement.
propositions.quote: The prices paid by Glaxo Canada to Adechsa were a payment for a bundle of at least some rights and benefits under the Licence Agreement and product under the Supply Agreement.

paragraphs.summary: Considering Licence and Supply agreements together reflects Glaxo Canada’s secondary role and payments for rights and product.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. erred refusing to consider Licence Agreement, leading to flawed comparable price finding.
propositions.quote: Rip A.C.J. erred in refusing to take account of the Licence Agreement. It was that refusal which led him to find that the prices the generic pharmaceutical companies paid for ranitidine were comparable under the CUP method.

propositions.text: Generic comparators do not reflect Glaxo Canada’s economic and business reality and do not indicate reasonable price without adjustment.
propositions.quote: the generic comparators do not reflect the economic and business reality of Glaxo Canada and, at least without adjustment, do not indicate the price that would be reasonable in the circumstances, had Glaxo Canada and Adechsa been dealing at arm’s length.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Rip A.C.J. erred by ignoring Licence Agreement; generic comparators don’t reflect Glaxo Canada’s reality or reasonable price.

propositions.text: Reasonable amount if Glaxo Canada and Adechsa dealt at arm’s length remains to be determined.
propositions.quote: “the amount that would have been reasonable in the circumstances” if Glaxo Canada and Adechsa had been dealing at arm’s length has yet to be determined (para. 79).

propositions.text: Determination requires close examination of Licence Agreement terms and rights granted to Glaxo Canada.
propositions.quote: This will require a close examination of the terms of the Licence Agreement and the rights and benefits granted to Glaxo Canada under that Agreement.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees reasonable arm’s length price remains undetermined and requires close Licence Agreement examination.

propositions.text: Licence Agreement clause 11(1)(b) states no royalties payable by Glaxo Canada on purchases from Group or Associates, only on net sales.
propositions.quote: the Licence Agreement expressly provides under clause 11(1)(b): (ii) in the event that Glaxo Canada purchases raw materials or bulk or finished Product from GROUP or an Associate it is the parties’ express intention that no royalties be payable by Glaxo Canada on the importation of such raw materials or bulk or finished Product but only on GLAXO CANADA’s Net Sales of Product in the Territory;

propositions.text: No royalties payable as condition of sale by Group or Associates to Glaxo Canada for export merchandise, priced separately.
propositions.quote: (iii) Glaxo Canada shall not be required to pay any royalty or license fee as a condition of the sale by Group or its Associates to Glaxo Canada of merchandise for export to the Territory and such merchandise shall be priced in accordance with a separate agreement between the parties without regard to royalties payable hereunder

propositions.text: No royalty payable on manufacture or use of Products, only on sales.
propositions.quote: (iv) no royalty shall be payable by Glaxo Canada on its manufacture or use of the Products but only on its sales of the Products;

paragraphs.summary: Licence Agreement states Glaxo Canada pays no royalties on purchases or manufacture, only on net sales, per clause 11(1)(b).

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada did not rely on s. 212(1)(d) or s. 215(1) regarding tax on royalties or withholding tax.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Canada’s pleadings in the Tax Court did not rely on s. 212(1) (d) or s. 215(1) of the Act , which provide for tax payable by non-residents on royalties or similar payments for the right to use any patent or trademark in Canada and for withholding tax on behalf of the non-resident.

propositions.text: No evidence Glaxo Canada withheld amounts for royalties paid to Adechsa.
propositions.quote: There is no evidence that Glaxo Canada withheld any amounts of the prices it paid to Adechsa in respect of royalties for the use or the right to use the ranitidine patent or Zantac trademark.

paragraphs.summary: Glaxo Canada did not rely on tax provisions for royalties and no evidence of withholding on royalties paid to Adechsa.

propositions.text: No determination made whether patent and trademark rights are linked to purchase price paid to Adechsa.
propositions.quote: I make no determination in these reasons as to whether the rights under the ranitidine patent granted to Glaxo Canada to manufacture and sell Zantac and the exclusive right to use the Zantac trademark are linked to the purchase price paid by Glaxo Canada to Adechsa.

propositions.text: If purchase price includes compensation for IP rights, consistency with withholding tax position is required.
propositions.quote: if the purchase price includes compensation for intellectual property rights granted to Glaxo Canada, there would have to be consistency between that and Glaxo Canada’s position with respect to Part XIII withholding tax.

propositions.text: Issue not argued here; may be addressed in Tax Court later.
propositions.quote: This issue was not specifically argued in this Court and may be addressed by the parties in the Tax Court and considered by the Tax Court judge when considering whether any specific rights and benefits conferred on Glaxo Canada under the Licence Agreement are linked to the price for ranitidine paid to Adechsa.

paragraphs.summary: Court makes no determination on IP rights link to price; notes withholding tax consistency issue not argued and may be addressed later.

propositions.text: Licence Agreement grants rights and benefits beyond patent and trademark, e.g. access to new products, supply rights, marketing support, technical assistance.
propositions.quote: there are rights and benefits under the Licence Agreement referred to in para. 7 above, other than the patent and trademark rights granted to Glaxo Canada. For example, guaranteed access to new products, the right to the supply of raw materials and materials in bulk, marketing support, and technical assistance for setting up new product lines all appear to have some value.

paragraphs.summary: Licence Agreement includes valuable rights beyond IP, such as product access, supply, marketing support, and technical assistance.

propositions.text: Rip A.C.J. found Adechsa’s ranitidine under Glaxo Group’s GMP may confer comfort of minimal impurities and responsible manufacture.
propositions.quote: Adechsa’s ranitidine manufactured under Glaxo Group’s “good manufacturing practices” “may confer a certain degree of comfort that the good has minimal impurities and is manufactured in a responsible manner” (para. 118).

propositions.text: Zantac is priced higher than generic products, partly due to this comfort value.
propositions.quote: Zantac is priced higher than the generic products, presumably, at least in part, because of that “degree of comfort” that Rip A.C.J. acknowledged.

paragraphs.summary: Rip A.C.J. found Adechsa’s ranitidine under GMP adds comfort; Zantac’s higher price partly reflects this, court notes.

propositions.text: Licence Agreement features and purchase source add value beyond generic ranitidine, justifying recognition in arm’s length price.
propositions.quote: These are all features of the Licence Agreement and the requirement to purchase from a Glaxo-approved source that add value to the ranitidine that Glaxo Canada purchased from Adechsa over and above the value of generic ranitidine without these rights and benefits.

propositions.text: Only after identifying Licence Agreement circumstances linked to Supply Agreement can arm’s length comparisons be determined.
propositions.quote: It is only after identifying the circumstances arising from the Licence Agreement that are linked to the Supply Agreement that arm’s length comparisons under any of the OECD methods or other methods may be determined.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Licence Agreement features add value justifying recognition; arm’s length comparisons require identifying linked circumstances first.

propositions.text: Section 69(2) uses 'reasonable amount' reflecting transfer pricing is not exact science, allowing leeway in determining reasonable amount.
propositions.quote: s. 69(2) uses the term “reasonable amount”. This reflects the fact that, to use the words of the 1995 Guidelines, “transfer pricing is not an exact science” (para. 1.45).

propositions.text: If transfer price is within reasonable range, section requirements are satisfied; court may select point within reasonable range using statistical measures.
propositions.quote: As long as a transfer price is within what the court determines is a reasonable range, the requirements of the section should be satisfied. If it is not, the court might select a point within a range it considers reasonable in the circumstances based on an average, median, mode, or other appropriate statistical measure

propositions.text: Comparators will rarely be identical; Tax Court judge must exercise best informed judgment to establish arm’s length price.
propositions.quote: it is highly unlikely that any comparisons will yield identical circumstances and the Tax Court judge will be required to exercise his best informed judgment in establishing a satisfactory arm’s length price.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 69(2) allows leeway in transfer pricing, requiring best judgment to find a reasonable arm’s length price within a range.

propositions.text: Assessment of evidence is for trial judge, considering roles of Glaxo Canada and Glaxo Group in transfer pricing.
propositions.quote: assessment of the evidence is a matter for the trial judge, I would observe that the respective roles and functions of Glaxo Canada and the Glaxo Group should be kept in mind.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada does secondary manufacturing and marketing; Glaxo Group owns IP and provides rights and benefits.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Canada engaged in the secondary manufacturing and marketing of Zantac. Glaxo Group is the owner of the intellectual property and provided other rights and benefits to Glaxo Canada.

propositions.text: Transfer pricing must not misallocate earnings ignoring different functions, resources, and risks of each party.
propositions.quote: Transfer pricing should not result in a misallocation of earnings that fails to take account of these different functions and the resources and risks inherent in each.

propositions.text: Whether compensation for intellectual property rights is justified is for Tax Court judge to determine.
propositions.quote: whether or not compensation for intellectual property rights is justified in this particular case is a matter for determination by the Tax Court judge.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the trial judge must assess evidence considering Glaxo Canada’s and Glaxo Group’s roles and IP compensation justification.

propositions.text: Arm’s length prices consider independent interests of both parties; both Glaxo Group and Glaxo Canada interests must be considered.
propositions.quote: prices between parties dealing at arm’s length will be established having regard to the independent interests of each party to the transaction. That means that the interests of Glaxo Group and Glaxo Canada must both be considered.

propositions.text: An appropriate arm’s length test determination under s. 69(2) should reflect these realities.
propositions.quote: An appropriate determination under the arm’s length test of s. 69(2) should reflect these realities.

paragraphs.summary: The court says arm’s length pricing must consider both parties’ interests and reflect these realities under s. 69(2).

propositions.text: Evidence shows arm’s length distributors prefer acquiring ranitidine from Glaxo Group supplier over generic sources.
propositions.quote: there is some evidence that indicates that arm’s length distributors have found it in their interest to acquire ranitidine from a Glaxo Group supplier, rather than from generic sources.

propositions.text: Higher-than-generic transfer prices may be justified and not necessarily unreasonable under s. 69(2).
propositions.quote: This suggests that higher-than-generic transfer prices are justified and are not necessarily greater than a reasonable amount under s. 69(2).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence suggests higher-than-generic transfer prices may be justified and reasonable under s. 69(2).

propositions.text: Dismiss appeal and cross-appeal and remit matter to Rip A.C.J. for redetermination.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the appeal, and for the reasons below, dismiss the cross-appeal and remit the matter to Rip A.C.J. (now Chief Justice) for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: The court would dismiss both appeal and cross-appeal and remit the matter for redetermination.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada cross-appeals to overturn Federal Court of Appeal’s remittance to Tax Court for redetermination.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Canada cross-appeals, arguing that the decision of the Federal Court of Appeal to remit the matter to the Tax Court for redetermination should be overturned.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada asks Court to set aside reassessment, claiming it satisfied burden by demolishing Minister’s assumptions.
propositions.quote: It asks this Court to set aside the reassessment on the basis that it has satisfied its burden as a taxpayer because it has “demolished” the assumptions of the Minister.

paragraphs.summary: Glaxo Canada cross-appeals, arguing it satisfied its burden and the reassessment should be set aside.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal remitted matter to Tax Court as Glaxo Canada failed to show prices paid were reasonable under s. 69(2).
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal remitted the matter to the Tax Court on the basis that Glaxo Canada had not discharged its burden of demonstrating that the prices it paid Adechsa for ranitidine were reasonable under s. 69(2)

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal found Judge erred in law by not applying proper test for reasonable amount if parties were at arm’s length.
propositions.quote: I conclude that the Judge erred in law in failing to apply the proper test in determining “the amount that would have been reasonable in the circumstances” if the appellant and Adechsa had been dealing at arm’s length.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal declined to determine reasonable amount, remitting to Tax Court to consider record adequacy or need for more evidence.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal declined to make such a determination on the basis that it could not properly assess the adequacy of the record on this point and remitted the matter to the Tax Court judge to consider whether a decision can be made on the basis of the existing record or whether additional evidence is necessary.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court of Appeal remitted matter to Tax Court for redetermination, finding Judge erred and record inadequate for determination.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada argues Minister’s choice of generic comparators is basis of assessment; burden was to show generic transactions not proper comparator.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Canada argues that the choice of the generic comparator transactions by the Minister constitutes the basis of the Minister’s assessment. Therefore, the burden on Glaxo Canada was only to demonstrate that the transactions of the generic pharmaceutical companies were not the proper comparator.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada says demolishing comparator basis would discharge its burden.
propositions.quote: In Glaxo Canada’s view, such a finding would demolish the basis of the assessment, thus, discharging its burden.

paragraphs.summary: Glaxo Canada argues burden was only to show generic comparators were improper, which would demolish assessment basis.

propositions.text: Minister says basis of assessment is that prices paid were not reasonable; generic comparators were just a means to show unreasonableness.
propositions.quote: The Minister argues that the basis of the assessment was the determination that the prices Glaxo Canada paid for ranitidine were not reasonable. The selection of the generic comparators was only a means which the Minister had chosen to demonstrate the unreasonableness.

paragraphs.summary: Minister argues assessment basis is unreasonableness of prices paid, not choice of generic comparators.

propositions.text: Basis of assessment found in Minister’s Amended Reply assumptions 14p) and 14r.A).
propositions.quote: The basis of the assessment is found in the assumptions in the Minister’s Amended Reply to Glaxo Canada’s Amended Notice of Appeal. Assumptions 14p) and r.A) provide: p) the Appellant paid Adechsa, with whom it was not dealing at arm’s length, a price for ranitidine which was greater than the amount that would have been reasonable in the circumstances if the Appellant and Adechsa had been dealing at arm’s length; r.A) any amounts paid by the appellant to Adechsa over and above the prices paid by other Canadian pharmaceutical companies (as detailed in Schedule A attached) were not for the supply of ranitidine;

paragraphs.summary: Court states basis of assessment is assumptions 14p) and 14r.A) in Minister’s Amended Reply.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada argues only assumption 14r.A) is basis of assessment and it demolished that assumption.
propositions.quote: Glaxo Canada argues, in effect, that only assumption 14r.A) constitutes the basis of the assessment and that it has demolished that assumption.

propositions.text: Minister argues basis of assessment is assumption 14p).
propositions.quote: The Minister argues that the basis of the assessment is assumption 14p).

propositions.text: Text supports Minister’s position that assumption 14p) sets statutory basis for reassessment under s. 69(2).
propositions.quote: The text of the assumptions supports the position of the Minister. Here assumption 14p) sets out the statutory basis for the reassessment, placing the reassessment squarely under s. 69(2).

propositions.text: Taxpayer’s liability governed by Act; Minister’s reassessment authority arises from invoking specific Act provisions.
propositions.quote: The taxpayer’s liability is governed by the Act and the Minister’s authority to reassess arises from invoking a particular provision or provisions of the Act .

paragraphs.summary: Glaxo Canada says only assumption 14r.A) is basis and demolished; Minister says 14p) is basis; court supports Minister’s view.

propositions.text: In Hickman Motors, taxpayer must demolish exact assumptions made by Minister but no more.
propositions.quote: In Hickman Motors Ltd. v. Canada, [1997] 2 S.C.R. 336, Justice L’Heureux-Dubé states that the taxpayer’s burden is to “‘demolish’ the exact assumptions made by the Minister but no more” (para. 92 (emphasis deleted)).

propositions.text: Assumption 14r.A) was demolished but assumption 14p) was not.
propositions.quote: Here, it is safe to say that assumption 14r.A) by the Minister of the prices paid by Apotex and Novopharm as CUP transactions, without adjustments, was indeed demolished. However, assumption 14p) was not.

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Hickman Motors: taxpayer must demolish exact assumptions; 14r.A) demolished but 14p) not demolished.

propositions.text: At Tax Court, Glaxo Canada tried to prove prices paid were reasonable but was unsuccessful.
propositions.quote: Indeed, at the Tax Court, Glaxo Canada sought to establish the reasonableness of the prices it paid, though its evidence and argument were not accepted by the Tax Court judge.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada accepted burden to show prices were reasonable under s. 69(2).
propositions.quote: In other words, it accepted the burden of demonstrating that the prices it paid were reasonable within the meaning of s. 69(2).

propositions.text: Had Glaxo Canada succeeded, assumptions 14p) and 14r.A) would have been demolished.
propositions.quote: Had it been successful in establishing that the prices it paid were reasonable, assumption 14p) as well as 14r.A), would have been demolished.

paragraphs.summary: Tax Court found Glaxo Canada failed to prove prices reasonable; had it succeeded, assumptions 14p) and 14r.A) would be demolished.

propositions.text: Assumption 14p) that prices paid were greater than reasonable amount remains undemolished.
propositions.quote: As it stands, the assumption that the prices paid by Glaxo Canada for ranitidine were greater than the amount that would have been reasonable in the circumstances, had Glaxo Canada and Adechsa been dealing at arm’s length, has not been demolished. Therefore, assumption 14p) remains standing.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds assumption 14p) remains standing as it was not demolished.

propositions.text: Glaxo Canada argued Federal Court of Appeal could determine reasonable amount.
propositions.quote: At the Federal Court of Appeal, Glaxo Canada argued that that court could determine “the reasonable amount”.

propositions.text: If Federal Court of Appeal could determine reasonable amount, it could remit matter to Tax Court for that determination.
propositions.quote: If the Federal Court of Appeal could determine the reasonable amount, I cannot see why it could not remit the matter to the Tax Court for that very determination.

paragraphs.summary: Glaxo Canada argued Federal Court of Appeal could determine reasonable amount; court finds it could remit to Tax Court for that.

propositions.text: Court would remit matter to Tax Court for redetermination considering Licence Agreement and any new evidence.
propositions.quote: Like the Federal Court of Appeal, I would remit the matter to the Tax Court to be redetermined, having regard to the effect of the Licence Agreement on the prices paid by Glaxo Canada for the supply of ranitidine from Adechsa. The Tax Court judge should consider any new evidence the parties seek to adduce and that he may choose to allow.

paragraphs.summary: Court would remit matter to Tax Court for redetermination considering Licence Agreement and new evidence.

propositions.text: Dismiss appeal with costs; dismiss cross-appeal with costs in this Court; remit to Tax Court for redetermination.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the appeal with costs throughout; dismiss the cross-appeal with costs in this Court and remit the matter to the Tax Court for redetermination. Appeal and cross-appeal dismissed with costs.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses appeal and cross-appeal with costs and remits matter to Tax Court for redetermination.
